Title: Designing and Implementing E2E Test Automation with Playwright

Instructor(s): Markku Niiranen, Senior Lecturer Enna Rissanen, Product Lead

This project examined the process of automating test cases for a software product, focusing on end-to-end (E2E) testing. The project was carried out for a client com- pany called Treanglo Oy. The aim was to develop test suites that reduce the work- load of human testers and ease with product release testing. The product has two sides, both of which were tested.

The project consisted of two phases: design and implementation. The design phase analysed the best testing strategies and the current state of E2E testing at Treanglo. Project specifications and risk prevention plans were detailed to provide a clear scope and ease with implementation. Test suites were developed in the implementa- tion phase, with the goal of testing critical user behaviour on both sides of the prod- uct. Test data management was comprehensively implemented to keep the test envi- ronment clean. In addition, future development plans were outlined.

The results demonstrate that test automation improves testing efficiency. Although the project only handled critical desktop browser test cases, it provides an important tool for release testing. Additionally, it demonstrates a solid automation base that can be expanded and combined with existing unit and integration tests. In conclusion, the study illustrates the need for test automation in modern software development.

Keywords: automation, testing, software development

# Introduction

As the modern world becomes increasingly software-driven and products shift toward online solutions, the need for software testing grows. Web applications must now be validated for multiple browsers, screen sizes and devices, making manual testing even for simple products extremely time- and labour-intensive. Automated end-to-end (E2E) tests provide simulated, pre-determined user inter- actions in a fraction of the time required for manual testing. They are consistent, repeatable and reliable, following identical patterns of behaviour each time.

This final year project was carried out as part of Treanglo Oy's test automation development project. The primary objective was to streamline the E2E testing of Treanglo's growing online sales platform and provide an acceptance testing tool. As a mid-sized company with a small testing team and a product offering a wide range of features and functionality, the current manual-only E2E testing may take multiple days. Manual testing places a significant strain on the release cycle and testers, the repetitive nature of the tests easily leading to fatigue in humans. This increases the chance of bugs going unnoticed and reaching pro- duction.

The product has two sides: public, open-to-all Kide.app and Kide.admin, which is exclusively for approved administrative users. The product offers a significant variety of features, including multiple payment methods as well as delivery and product options, and a customisable product listing setup. Release testing of the product is exhaustive and detailed, often testing the same behaviour multiple times but with one variable modified.

This study examines the process of planning, designing, and implementing a base for improved E2E test automation for Treanglo's product. It consists of seven chapters. Following the introduction, Chapter 2 presents background for software test automation as well as the company and product and analyses of the current state of E2E test suites at the company. Chapter 3 outlines project specifications and risks and limitations. Chapter 4 gives an overview of the tools

and technologies utilised and Chapter 5 details the final implementation. Chap- ter 6 explores future development. Finally, Chapter 7 reviews the project and its objectives.

# Background

Although established E2E test automation already exists at Treanglo, it is pres- ently not in use. Its development was halted after major problems were identi- fied during a code review. Currently, the test automation team is evaluating whether the existing suites should be kept and heavily modified or if a complete overhaul of the codebase is required. This chapter presents an overview of soft- ware test automation and introduces both the company and product. Addition- ally, the concept of seeded entities is defined and the current state of E2E test automation at Treanglo is analysed.

### Software Test Automation

According to the International Software Testing Qualifications Board (ISTQB), test automation is the practice of using software tools to execute tests and com- pare the outcomes with expected results without requiring manual intervention at each step \[1\]. Automated tests confirm the software fulfils predefined require- ments for application functionality and user experience \[2\].

Test automation is critical in modern software development, as it reduces hu- man error and considerably speeds up testing. As systems become increasingly more complex and integrated, even with best practices implemented for manual testing, some human error is inevitable. In a worst-case scenario, they may re- sult in bugs and errors reaching production.

In software test automation, technical concepts rarely have generalized stand- ards. Instead, the current state is often determined by commercial tool manufac- turers and open-source communities. These parties are often more driven to create competitive advantage or develop new features than to implementing

generalized standards. Nevertheless, automated testing has a few largely ac- cepted standards and methods related to the design, organisation, and execu- tion. \[3.\]

One of these is the Test Pyramid. In 2009, Mike Cohn introduced the concept in his book "Succeeding with Agile" \[4\]. The primary aim was to aid in balancing test automation needs, the model visualising the different layers of software testing \[4\]. Each layer indicates the relative number of tests, with lower layers containing more than higher layers \[2\]. The model consists of three layers (from bottom to top): unit tests, service tests and UI tests \[4\].

Several years later, a new version of the pyramid was proposed by Ham Vocke: the Practical Test Pyramid \[4\]. While this model keeps unit tests as the largest category, it replaces service tests with integration tests and UI tests with E2E tests. Additionally, manual testing is included as an informal layer.

The Practical Test Pyramid has since become popularized as the standard model for software test automation. It is known as simply the Test Pyramid in modern test automation. The figure below visualizes the model.

![A pyramid divided into three horizontally. Bottom layer is labelled ](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 1. The Practical Test Pyramid model. Adapted from Ham Vocke \[4\].

Figure 1 visualises the four layers of test automation as a pyramid. The lowest layer contains unit tests, the middle integration tests, and the top E2E tests. The size of the layer correlates to the number of tests each category should have, unit test having the most and E2E tests the least. Manual tests are an unofficial cloud layer, separated from the rest of the pyramid model.

Unit testing validates the smallest individual parts of the codebase. Unit tests verify the behaviour of a specific function or method in the application. They test the base functionality of code and should be independent and isolated. \[5.\]

Integration testing verifies the interactions and data exchange between the components and modules of an application \[6\]. It ensures that separately devel- oped parts of the code function together as a larger system and detects issues that arise from their interactions.

End-to-end testing validates that the integrated components (e.g. front-end, da- tabases, APIs) work correctly together, providing a full beginning-to-end view of application behaviour \[7\]. They strive to mimic real-world scenarios, examining the user experience. E2E tests are by nature often complex and time-consum- ing, in both developing and executing \[9\]. There should be the least relative number of E2E tests in a full automation system, thus its placement on top of the pyramid.

Finally, manual tests are performed step-by-step by a human tester. Although test automation focuses on automated processes, manual testing is sometimes unavoidable and must be acknowledged. Manual tests should be kept minimal and automated wherever possible. They are visualised as a cloud in figure 1, unofficial but prepared for. \[2.\]

While the Test Pyramid is the standard form of software test automation, it is not without issues. Large suites of unit tests often do not function well in modern software applications, especially those that undergo frequent changes (such as startup development environments). Even minor code refactoring may lead to unit tests failing falsely. This causes high maintenance costs, when unit tests might have to be frequently modified to work properly with the new code. \[8.\]

The Test Diamond Model suggested by Dusko Bajic is an evolution of the tradi- tional test pyramid. This model prioritizes integration testing over unit testing. It is especially suitable for applications that heavily depend on system integrations such as APIs and databases. The figure below illustrates the model. \[9.\]

![A diamond divided into three layers horizontally. Bottom layer is labelled ](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 2. Test Diamond model. Adapted from Bajic \[9\].

Figure 2 visualises the Test Diamond model. Rather than having the unit tests as the largest layer, they have been reduced to the same size as E2E tests. In this model, unit tests only cover the most critical aspects, decreasing the need for meticulous maintenance \[9\].

Instead, integration tests in the middle become the largest layer. In this model, the most significance is placed on system integrations to prioritise business-crit- ical functionality \[10\]. Since third-party integrations are especially susceptible to failing and leading to system-wide issues, the diamond reduces the number of unit tests in exchange of comprehensively testing system interactions and data

exchange \[10\]. This is the test automation model that Treanglo's test automa- tion strategy utilises, for the emphasis on integration while reducing unit mainte- nance costs.

Both open source and commercial frameworks and browser automation libraries exist as tools for software test automation, including Selenium, Playwright, and Robot Framework. E2E testing of native applications require their own frame- works and libraries, such as Appium. As this thesis focuses on web browser testing, native application testing will not be further elaborated on.

While the final decision of tools requires more in-depth research, for the pur- poses of this project either Selenium or Playwright currently seem like the best option. Selenium is older and more established in the test automation industry, while Playwright is newer and developed at a rapid pace.

The current E2E test automation uses Selenium minimally, but it could be uti- lised better. It is an open-source umbrella project for a range of tools and librar- ies that enable and support the automation of web browsers. If the current test automation is only modified, Selenium will be kept. \[11.\]

If the system is completely overhauled, the open-source web automation frame- work Playwright has been considered as replacement \[12\]. Playwright's test runner has been built specifically for E2E testing, making it a strong candidate. With its cross-browser automation using one API, Playwright could be the best tool for this project \[12\].

### Company and Product

Treanglo Oy is a Finnish technology company founded in 2014. It is best known for Kide.app and Kide.admin, all-in-one mobile and online platform for event management and web shop services \[13\]. Although they are often directly re- ferred to as just Kide.app, the two platforms serve the same product from differ- ent perspectives with major differences in functionality.

Kide.app, Treanglo's flagship product, is a well-established online event sale platform among higher education students in Finland. With over 500 seller or- ganisations and around 220,000 active monthly users \[14\], Kide.app reaches tens of thousands of customers weekly \[15\].

The users (also known as end users) of Kide.app can buy products such as event tickets, overall patches, and student union and association memberships. The application also hosts an official, Kela-approved student card that can be used to receive student discounts in Finland. One in five working-age Finns have used Kide.app, making it one of Finland's most recognisable brands among 18-35-year-olds \[16\]. Kide.app can be accessed through hybrid native mobile applications (for iOS and Android) and web browser.

Kide.app is the better-known side of the platform, open for anyone with a regis- tered account, while Kide.admin is exclusively for sellers (hereinafter referred to as admins). When creating a new organisation account, the information listed (e.g. business ID, organization email and address) must be manually approved by a Treanglo employee.

After the organization account has been approved, personal administrative ac- counts can be attached to it. Admins can create and manage organization prod- ucts, which are automatically listed for sale on Kide.app. Additionally, they can host and import membership registries, mass-email buyers, and manage deliv- ery options. The Kide.admin platform does not have mobile applications and can currently only be used through web browser.

Founded through a bachelor's thesis project, the main goal of Kide.app was to simplify the process of selling event tickets and memberships for student asso- ciations. Although other ticket selling platforms existed (e.g. Lippu.fi, Tiketti), these platforms were not suitable for student associations according to founder and CEO Kassu La Habana Reyes \[17\]. The competitors of the time were too expensive for student associations to use, the servers could not handle large amounts of traffic, and they were not mobile phone compatible \[17\].

Before Kide.app (then known as Bailataan), student associations had to sell their products exclusively in campus offices and events, limiting sale periods. La Habana Reyes and his co-founders aimed to solve this problem, inspired by their own experiences in student association boards \[17\]. Kide.app allowed stu- dent associations and unions to sell their tickets online and continuously, until the tickets ran out. Any buyer no matter their location could now just open the application when sales started and secure their tickets.

Due to its beginnings, the platform's current biggest merchants are student as- sociations and unions or singular large-scale student events \[18\]. Most student events in Finland today are sold at least partly through Kide.app, and 80-90% of the users are higher education students \[17\]. However, Kide.app's reach has expanded in the past years and now includes nightclubs, sporting events, and festivals such as Weekend Festival as sellers. It has also expanded to operate in Estonia, Germany, and most recently, Austria.

### Defining Seeded Entities

The term "seeded entity" refers to data objects and concepts within a system that are created using default values instead of user created data \[19\]. They are integral for organizing and managing automation test data. In this project, the term is used for test data objects that are pre-populated (hereinafter referred to as seeded) during test execution. Rather than relying on pre-existing or hard- coded entities, seeded entities provide new unique test data created during the setup of each execution using automated scripts. \[20\]

User, admin, and organisation accounts, products and variants, as well as deliv- ery methods are all entities within this system. They all have a unique ID that distinguishes them from each other and are easily searchable. They contain

key-value pairs that describe their properties and possible relationships to other entities. For example, the end and admin user share fields such as email, name, and password, but admin accounts will always be a part of an organisa- tion while the end users are independent. \[20.\]

### Current State Analysis

Beginning the project, Treanglo already had an E2E test automation system in development. The original plan was to move on to Phase 2 but the code review for Phase 1 uncovered major issues with the system. These issues will be elab- orated upon later in the section.

In this system, all testing (both manual and automated) was performed in an Az- ure test environment that simulates the Kide.app and Kide.admin platforms with test data. All code from developers was pushed to the environment for review and it was the last step before a new functionality is published to production.

The figure below illustrates the publishing flow, defining where the testing envi- ronment was in the flow.

![Three boxes in are in row, fourth box below the middle box. Far-left box labelled ](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 3. Kide.app web browser publishing flow.

Figure 3 illustrates the publishing flow for web browsers. First, a developer worked on the code in their own local environment, which was a branch of the DEV (development) environment. When the code was ready, it was pushed from DEV to the test environment. If the new functionality performed according to the acceptance testing requirements, it was pushed to production for real us- ers.

Both backend and front-end environments were hosted within the Azure test en- vironment in separate containers. This allowed the test environment to closely mimic production. Test automation used the test environment to execute test

suites. A private GitLab repository was used for test automation version control although no automation pipelines had been utilised. The backlog and any avail- able documentation of test cases was hosted on Notion (a task management and note taking application).

This test automation focused exclusively on critical E2E web browser test auto- mation for the time being as testing mobile applications required the use of a separate specialised framework. Additionally, access to development environ- ments had not been granted to the test automation team and thus unit or inte- gration tests could not be implemented. Individual unit and integration tests had been implemented by the product software developers, but no documentation existed on their purpose or functionality. These tests were and still are isolated from rest of test automation.

As mentioned before, major issues arose during a code review which caused the development of E2E test automation to be halted. A total of 52 test cases had been implemented by the time the development was paused in late-Novem- ber 2025. The most significant of these issues related to rigid data manage- ment, a bloated codebase, and code execution. The severity of these issues meant a decision had to be made before the thesis project could be started: should the existing system be kept and possibly heavily modified or should it be scrapped and started over from the beginning?

The rigidity of test data management was caused by using hardcoded product IDs and credentials. Originally, E2E test automation relied heavily on these, ex- cept for tests specifically for new entity creation. They were used to repeatedly access the same entities in the test environment, creating unnecessary depend- encies and possible access conflicts. For example, if a critical entity were acci- dentally deleted, it could easily break several tests that depend on it. Although no issues ever occurred, this is not a sustainable long-term approach for a team of more than one developer and introduces easily avoidable risks.

API request-based entity management was eventually implemented across E2E test automation, not long before the development was halted. This method ena- bled the creation, seeding, and removal of test case specific entities through API requests. It provided new test entities while still maintaining data hygiene.

Additional research had to still be done before the beginning of this thesis pro- ject but API request-based management was a viable solution despite the level of changes that would be implemented.

The bloated codebase created its own issues. As implementation was not planned prior to beginning the development and software test automation had been a new concept to its only developer, the helpers and test cases were not consistent in functionality. A significant part of the bloat was caused by underuti- lising Selenium libraries and instead implementing a mostly custom framework. The product's functionality was not specialised enough to warrant a custom framework to this degree.

There were also many cases of two helper actions fulfilling the same functional- ity but in slightly differing ways. Often the old actions could not even be re- moved when identified, as they were critical for the functionality of other, earlier tests. Furthermore, test cases implemented earlier into the development pro- cess could greatly differ in logic from tests developed later. Due to the incon- sistent coding standards and bloat, the codebase could be extremely difficult to navigate.

Finally, executing test suites was done completely manually through a remotely installed branch. The selection of test modules (or happy paths) that contained the suites to be executed was defined in a Program.cs file, where all existing test modules were listed as individual run commands. These commands were enabled and disabled through commenting or uncommenting run commands, with only the uncommented lines being included in program execution. Finally, the run would be manually initiated through the integrated development environ- ment (IDE).

Using comments to manage test suite execution is not a best practise or sus- tainable long-term. As more test suites would be added, the list would become longer and more difficult to navigate.

# Project Specifications

Following careful deliberation, a complete overhaul of E2E test automation was undertaken. This means the scope now included configuring the codebase and test data management (TDM), especially for seeded entities, along with imple- menting minimum viable product (MVP) requirements. The new system had to also utilise user stories in test case development and provide feedback for de- velopers as quickly as possible. While some tests would be more time-consum- ing than others, the system had to utilise parallel execution to run all imple- mented test suites as quickly as possible.

The scope and MVP of this project corresponded to the first phase of the overall test automation redevelopment project. Development begun in January and the deadline was set April 30th. In this chapter, the scope of the first phase is de- fined, the limitations and risks of the project identified, and mitigation strategies disclosed.

### Project Scope

New E2E test automation was to be designed and implemented to support re- gression testing the most critical aspects of product functionality. The test auto- mation project had two primary objectives: create a tool for web browser release testing as well as provide clear and relatively quick feedback for the developer on full product functionality. The scope did not include mobile browser or appli- cation testing, instead prioritising desktop browser regression testing to create a solid base for test automation and to keep the number of test suites to imple- ment achievable. Furthermore, the scope focused exclusively on E2E testing due to factors elaborated later in the thesis.

Reaching MVP required implementing 80% of all critical test cases (both admin and end-user) and all team members gaining access to the codebase to be able to execute tests locally. To fulfil the critical test case implementation require- ment, 80% of all critical test cases had to be implemented and passed reliably. Access for all members required creating clear and accessible documentation, including instructions for cloning the repository locally, installing required pack- ages, and configuring correct credentials to a .env file.

The existing publishing flow would not be changed, the E2E test automation op- erating within the Azure test environment. Existing test data management and version control practises would be kept, modified for the purposes of this project scope. Finally, the decision was made to adopt to Playwright as the testing framework, replacing Selenium. Both test data management and Playwright will be discussed in detail in the following sections.

### Limitations and Risks

As is common with all projects, there were limitations and risks. For this project, two significant limitations were identified, along with multiple risks, which had to be mitigated as thoroughly as possible. This section will outline the limitations and risks as well as the plans to solve or reduce their impact.

With Treanglo's test automation being completely overhauled, one significant limitation came with test data management. While the original plan consisted of using a test database, that is re-seeded every time test suites are executed, the backend team's technical debt was too large for any new tasks. This limitation was solved by utilizing API requests for entity management, similar to the previ- ous E2E test automation system. The next chapter will discuss TDM in detail.

The other limitation arose with unit and integration testing. While usually test au- tomation tools would implement unit and integration tests before E2E, the test automation team did not have access to the development codebase. Therefore, unit and integration testing of the product codebase was not possible. However,

E2E web browser testing required only the use of the test environment user in- terface (UI). With the summer period being an extremely busy season for prod- uct development, the decision was made to focus on E2E to create a tool for re- lease testing and reduce the workload on human testers.

One of the biggest risks of the project was the amount of test cases to be imple- mented. Test cases were written based on user stories, meaning the critical sto- ries had to be identified and documented first. However, the user stories library was being revamped by the project manager at the beginning of the project, and not all critical stories had been documented yet. This meant that while MVP re- quired 80% of critical test cases to be implemented, a definite number of cases could not be defined at the time.

This was mitigated by having the project manager prioritise critical user stories, so that they could be listed by March 2026. Though the implementation phase was started in January 2026, 18 relevant user stories had already been defined at the time of writing this. The March deadline provided two additional months for the product manager and was around two months before the test automation project deadline. A preliminary estimation of relevant critical user stories was around 30-35, which would translate to 35-50 test cases. This would give enough time for MVP implementation.

Another risk surrounded Playwright, the test automation framework chosen. It was completely new for the test automation team, which meant a steeper learn- ing curve for the developers. This could lead to slower implementation and in- crease the risk of using bad practises. To prevent this, the team was been given time to comprehensively research Playwright in the planning phase.

Lastly, the test automation development team consisted of only two developers. One worked part-time while the other was involved in another time-consuming project, although test automation was the primary project. The lack of human re- sources could pose an issue with getting all test cases implemented before the deadline.

# Tools and Technologies

This chapter covers the tools and technologies chosen for the project during the design process. It details how user stories will be utilised in developing test cases and reasons for selecting Playwright. Additionally, the current plans for test data management and GitLab are presented.

### Test Case Design Based on User Stories

User stories are a fundamental building block in both software development and testing. They define software functionality from user perspective, rather than technical, by stating what a user would do with the product to reach a goal.

They are a crucial method for developing E2E test cases, as they provide a de- sired product functionality to be tested. Test cases focus on fulfilling technical specifications for system behaviour, which easily allows for blind spots in user behaviour and functionality. User stories help bridge the gap by providing a guideline. \[21.\]

User stories had not been utilised in test automation at Treanglo before. In- stead, tests were implemented according to the test automation developer's dis- cretion or assigned by the product manager. This led to scattered test suites, with edge case tests sometimes being implemented long before basic function- ality. The overhaul of E2E test automation provided an ideal moment to imple- ment them into the development process. Going forward, user stories would be employed in the test case process from the beginning.

First, a user story is identified, defined, and documented by the product man- ager. They define what a user needs to do to reach a precise result. Addition- ally, acceptance criteria are provided, which specify what conditions must be met to fulfil the story. For example, a user story might be "As an end user, I can login using my email address so I can access my purchases". The acceptance criteria for this would be "requires submitting correct credentials (user exists with correct email and password)" and "user is not blocked or deleted".

For ease of categorization, the user stories utilize multiple tags:

- - - **Role**: Is the test from the point of view of an end-user or an admin user.
      - **Primary and secondary modules**: Stories are categorized by function- ality (e.g. orders, reservations and account).
      - **Priority**: The story is categorized as one of the following: P1 (Critical), P2 (High), P3 (Moderate), P4 (Low).
      - **Status**: The user story is either proposed, in review, or implemented.
      - **Linked test cases**: Links to the documentation of each test case that is applicable to the user story.

Test cases are then written based on the story. One user story, which describes the full user experience, will often be the basis for multiple test cases. The cases outline how the web browser must function for the test to be considered completed. For example, a "Login as end user" test case could be made from the previous user story, which would detail what needs to be accessed to log in. Additionally, it would contain functionality to validate the log in, such as having access to a menu page that is only visible to logged-in users.

The test cases are currently documented in a Notion database. They follow a tagging system for ease of identification. The test case template then has sec- tions for inputting a description, prerequisites, possible test data required, the test step-by-step, and expected outcomes. The identification tags are as fol- lows:

- - - **Priority level**: P1, P2, P3 or P4.
      - **User story**: Which user story the test case is derived from.
      - **Perspective**: Admin or end-user.
      - **Module**: Test cases are categorized by functionality (e.g. orders, reser- vations and account).
      - **Test name:** Name of the test suite file. Added when the test suite has been implemented.
      - **Expected status:** Success or fail.

Following this, the test case is added to the backlog of test cases to be auto- mated. In GitLab, an issue is created and added to the issue board, which func- tions as backlog, with the issue description including the full test case documen- tation. It is then added to a milestone based on the module as well as given a status tag (backlog, to do, in progress, in review).

When it is time to begin implementing a test case, a branch is created from the issue and cloned to be used locally. Once the test case has been implemented, it is submitted for code review, and the name of the test suite file is added to test case documentation. If the code is not accepted, the reviewer leaves de- tailed comments and suggestions for implementation. If the code is accepted, the merge request is accepted by a developer with high enough clearance and merged into the main branch.

### Playwright

Playwright is an open-source test automation framework for browser automation testing and web scraping developed by Microsoft \[22\]. It provides tools for test automation with the goal of making cross-browser E2E testing easier and more reliable \[22\]. Despite only being launched in January of 2020, it has quickly been established as a leading test automation framework.

As of 2026, Playwright has more than 84,000 stars on GitHub, and more than 450,000 repositories are dependent on the playwright-core package \[23\]. Multi- ple frameworks and libraries were considered but from the beginning, Play- wright was one of the top contenders alongside with Selenium.

While both had their strengths and weaknesses, Playwright pulled ahead by providing cross-browser testing with one API, a test generation tool, and de- tailed test reports. On the official Playwright website, the parallel execution and full isolation of Playwright tests as well as mobile browser automation (Android and iOS) are highlighted. It also provides an "auto wait" feature, which automati- cally attempts assertions until conditions are met to reduce test flakiness. \[24.\]

Playwright's APIRequestContext method allows sending requests to the server directly from Node.js without loading a page and running JavaScript code \[25\]. Playwright also supports testing Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit with a single API \[12\]. Additionally, the test runner provides full browser isolation, auto-wait- ing, and web-first assertions \[26\].

Tests can be generated automatically to a file through CodeGen extension \[27\]. CodeGen is a test generation tool that automatically creates test code by re- cording interactions on a web browser \[28\]. The figure below shows an example of Codegen in use.

![Two computer windows, one a Visual Code Studio file and one Playwright installation document. Visual Code Studio has red box around ](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 4. CodeGen in use \[28\].

Figure 4 is a screenshot of CodeGen in use. The window in the background is the web browser, and the smaller window in the foreground is a Visual Studio Code file. The web browser is a real page, which CodeGen analyses and rec- ords. It has a toolbar with six buttons, which is for managing the test generator tool (e.g. turn recorder off, generate locator names).

The recorded actions have been applied to the code in the smaller window. In the bottom left corner of the Visual Studio Code file, "Record at cursor" is out- lined in red. This allows actions to be recorded directly to wherever the cursor is at. If the "Record new" option above it was selected, the test generator tool would create a new test file and record the actions there.

Playwright also provides detailed test reports for debugging. Playwright Trace Viewer is a GUI tool that allows exploring recorded Playwright traces after a script has been executed for easier debugging \[29\]. It provides a full trace of the execution as a local PWA (Progressive Web App). PWA allows the view of the timeline and network requests, and the inspection of DOM (Document Object Model) snapshots for each action on a local machine. However, this method is performance heavy. By running a trace locally, they are recorded for each test run and can be viewed directly through a HTML (HyperText Markup Language) report on a local server. The figure below is an example of a Playwright HTML report. \[30.\]

![Localhost web page with test results divided by test and a general overview of test run. Tests are listed on top of each other and show test title, browser engine used for test, and runtime.](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 5. Playwright HTML report \[30\]

Figure 5 displays the layout of a Playwright HTML report. This is a less perfor- mance heavy view of the test, displaying a quick overview of basic information about the run for individual tests and in general. This includes test name, status, web engine used, and execution time.

The main section shows results for tests executed in a test suite file. Although six tests have been executed, the first three are for the same "has title" test while the last three are for a "get started link" test. The only difference between the three tests is the web browser engine (Chromium, Firefox and WebKit), indi- cated by the colourful browser tag on the right. Next to the tag is the amount of time each test took to execute (all around one second), while above them is the total run time of 7.8 seconds.

The text below the test title indicates which line of the file the test begins on. A green checkmark next to the titles shows that the tests passed as expected. On the top right side, a quick overview of the execution is provided. In this example, the total number of tests executed was six. All passed, none failed, and none

were flaky or skipped. Clicking one of the listed tests opens an individual report, which includes a detailed list of test steps and a trace file of that test.

Mobile browser automation will not be implemented in this scope but setting up proper mobile browser automation support for the future is critical. Although the native application is much more popular, an average of 22,300 users (~10%) access Kide.app via a browser each month \[31\]. Having mobile browser auto- mation support will be critical when mobile browser automation starts.

### Test Data Management

Test data management (TDM) is the general practice of creating, managing, and maintaining the data needed to perform software tests. It guarantees that accurate and consistent test data is available for all tests, leading to quicker and more reliable test execution. \[32.\]

TDM enables test isolation by creating unique but valid data, ensuring that vali- dation and testing remain meaningful by following production data conventions \[32\]. Proper TDM is always important, but especially in this system as it handles large amounts of test data and entities. In this project, test fixtures were used to inject and manage dependencies that perform TDM (especially for entities).

Fixtures are Playwright's dependency injection system, providing a way to set up test environments and share objects between tests. Fixtures allow for isola- tion between tests, providing each test its own controlled set up rather than rely- ing on a shared state. In Playwright, fixtures encapsulate the setup and teardown of test dependencies, providing everything required for test execution without unnecessary overhead. They are reusable, on-demand and flexible \[33.\]

"Reusable" means that the fixtures can be defined once and used in multiple tests. If a helped function is used in multiple tests, it might be optimal to turn into a fixture. For example, Playwright provides a built-in page fixture which auto- matically creates a Page object for interacting with the browser, such as creat- ing an isolated page for each test. \[33.\]

"On-demand" refers to the way multiple fixtures can be defined but only those explicitly used in a test are initialized by Playwright. This speeds up and re- duces potential issues with test setup. \[33.\]

"Flexibility" describes how tests can tailor the environment to their needs and combine any fixtures without affecting other tests, unlike with helper methods. Playwright already offers several built-in test fixtures, including page, browser (a shared browser instance across tests), and request (an isolated APIRe- questContext instance for each run). \[33.\]

However, test fixtures were not the only form of test data management in this project. Entity management refers to the creation, population, storing, and re- moval of entities. Well-defined and implementation entity management was cru- cial, as proper unique data was paramount for the performance of the tests.

There are multiple approaches to managing entities, one of the most common being resetting or overwriting a test database before each execution. This ap- proach ensures all test data is cleared before the next test run, preventing lefto- ver data from accumulating and affecting the test environment. It is also rela- tively simple, as it requires minimal additional development effort from the test automation team.

However, creating and implementing a dedicated test database for this project was not possible due to the backend team's backlog and technical debt. In- stead, entity management was be handled using factory-like helper methods that utilize API requests for data creation. These methods were injected to the tests through test fixtures. Using API calls for entity management is fast, relia- ble, and scales well, especially for a test system that requires significant use of test data.

Although entities could be managed through the UI, this is not encouraged. Tests should not depend on step-by-step interactions for data set up. Addition- ally, hardcoding credentials is not considered best practice. This data does not adapt well to changes and slows test runtime.

### GitLab

As with the previous system, GitLab was utilized for the new test automation codebase. While previously it was only used for version control, the new test automation would utilize GitLab more comprehensively by implementing CI/CD and automation pipelines. The automation pipeline was implemented to check test stability and integration to the full system by executing all test suites when a merge request is made from a development branch to the main branch. The CI/CD pipeline was not implemented yet but will be done within 2026.

Additionally, research was done into moving bug reports to GitLab instead hav- ing them in a Notion database. Though reports and the CI/CD pipeline will not be implemented in this project, the goal is to have these implemented by Janu- ary 2027.

# Final Implementation

The first phase was scheduled to be completed by April 30th 2026, and as of mid-April, the goals of the first phase have been mostly completed. This chapter covers the final implementation of the test automation suites at the time of writ- ing, going over the system architecture, test fixtures as well as entity and test flakiness management.

### Test Automation System Architectures

The codebase architecture evolved through several iterations during the imple- mentation phase. File paths and architectural flows were adjusted, some com- ponents split or merged to improve efficiency, and others were removed com- pletely. The most significant change was the division of the codebase itself. Ini- tially, a single codebase was used for both Kide.app and Kide.admin test auto- mation, but this approach was soon recognised as impractical.

As a result, it was divided into two repositories: Kide E2E Public for Kide.app and Kide E2E Admin for Kide.admin. Both codebases follow similar architec- tures, so this chapter will not go over them separately. The figure below illus- trates the general codebase root folder setup.

![Five boxes, representative of root folder setup, are listed on top of each other, labelled (from top to bottom): Common, Constants, Data, Infrastructure, Tests. All boxes have 2-3 arrows, that point to their most important features.](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 6. Simplified high-level architecture diagram of the E2E test automation system.

Figure 6 is a simplified diagram of high-level E2E test automation system archi- tecture. It focuses on visualising the core setup of system functionality, instead of detailing each folder and file.

The root setup consists of five root folders: common, constants, data, infrastruc- ture, and tests. **Common** contains functionality for UI fixtures and Microsoft Graph. **Constants** include enums, models, and hardcoded test data. **Data** con- tains clients and factories, and **Infrastructure** flow fixtures and UI helpers.

**Tests** hosts the test suites as well as global teardown and setup. The root itself also includes individual configuration and package files, such as a placeholder file for an untracked .env file, but those are not visualized here.

The **Common** directory contains commonly used functionality, including a Mi- crosoft Graph folder which has helpers that allow accessing actual emails sent by Kide.app and Kide.admin. It also entails a fixture definition file for flows, so they can be used across the system.

The **Constants** directory contains shared, unchanging data used across the project. This includes enum definitions and related lookup mappings, model data structures for TypeScript interfaces and types (e.g. API request bases) and hardcoded test data, such as test credit card credentials. The directory also in- cludes global values such as site titles and URLs.

The **Data** directory is where most of the entity management is handled. It in- cludes a factory folder, which holds entity factories, builders, and registries to build seeded entities. The overarching folder is named factory, as the factories facilitate entity setup. Client files handle the creation of API requests and read the responses. Section 5.3 inspects entity management in full.

The **Infrastructure** directory contains the flow fixtures and UI helpers. Flows are for encapsulating specific UI interactions into reusable actions. UI helpers create step-by-step interactions with different browser sections (e.g. dialogs, menus and pages), providing helper methods for the flows to use. Section 5.2 discusses the use of fixtures and flows in detail.

Finally, the **tests** directory holds all the currently implemented test suites. Four test suites exist currently: account, authentication, orders, and reservations. Ac- count handles account state tests (e.g. creating a new account and changing password) while authentication is for login and logout related tests. Reserva- tions validate adding items to cart and checkout behaviour, while orders handle all payment tests. Additionally, the directory provides global setup and teardown files, which delete all seeded entities at the beginning and end of a run.

### Fixtures and Flows

Test fixtures are paramount for tests, as they are used to inject methods, de- pendencies, and actions to the test environment. In this project, both flows and factories are implemented as fixtures. Factories handle test data management and will be elaborated upon in the following section.

Flows provide reusable actions that combine interactions from page objects and other flows to perform high-level user and system behaviour, such as navigation and authentication. The page objects provide step-by-step UI interactions using locators to find and interact with page elements (the components of a webpage) \[34\]. Page objects are called by flows and focus exclusively on interaction logic. Any error handling is implemented on the flow level.

Flows help maintain succinct and readable test suites by providing tests actions. The figure below is an example of an action.

async openBrowserAndPerformLogin(

user: SeededUser, email?: string, password?: string

) {

if (email != null && password != null) { user.email = email;

user.password = password;

}

else if ( email != null { user.email = email;

}

else if (password != null) { user.password = password;

}

await this.commonFlow.openBrowser(); await this.topMenu.openLoginBrowser();

await this.loginDialog.performLogin(user);

await expect(this.loginSnackbar.loginSuccessfulSnackbar).toBeVis- ibile();

await this.topMenu.validateLogin();

}

Listing 1. A flow action to open a browser and login in a pre-existing user.

Listing 1 displays an implementation of an action in a flow. It illustrates how flows compile high-level actions by utilizing page objects for UI interactions or predefined actions from other flows. The action defines a full login action.

The commonFlow fixture and the topMenu page object are utilized to open a browser page and select the login dialog. A seeded user entity provides login credentials to input, and a snack bar indicating successful login is waited for un- til visible or the system times out. Finally, the state of login is validated by using the topMenu page object.

### Seeded Entity Management in Test Suites

Testing a sales platform requires the use of repeated, specific entities each time the test suites are run. While user accounts in Kide.app are independent enti- ties, most entities within Kide.admin belong to hierarchical dependencies and cannot be created in isolation. The hierarchy of dependencies is illustrated in the image below.

![Four levels. Bottom level has box labelled variant, third level has box labelled product, second level has boxes labelled delivery methods and admin next to each other, and top level has box labelled organization. variant points to product, product to admin, admin and delivery methods to organization.](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 7: Hierarchy of dependencies for Kide.admin entities.

Figure 7 presents the dependency chain for the Kide.admin entities. This covers organisations, admins, products, variants, and delivery methods. At the top of the hierarchy are organizations. Administrative accounts depend on organisa- tions, while products require an admin account to create them. Variant entities are the most dependent entity type, as they require an associated product.

Delivery methods have a varying dependency level: while creation requires only an organization, their use is partially dependent on variants. To effectively man- age entities, their lifecycles are handled through a combination of factories, cli- ents, builders, and registries. Together, they form a comprehensive and flexible TDM system and maintain good data hygiene. The figure below illustrates the flow of entity management during a test suite.

![Entity management in a test suite, starting from global setup and ending in global teardown. test suite asks function for an entity, function asks registry to find pre-existing or create new entity. If entity exists, it's given to test suite. If entity is created, client makes an API request, utilizing builder to populate a payload, which is saved to registry and given to test suite.](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 8. Entity Management Flow

Figure 8 illustrates the flow of entity management in a test suite. It consists of a test suite, entity factory, registry, client, builder and global setup and teardown.

The figure details how an entity is created, saved to a registry and removed. This management allows for the entity within a test suite run to be reused multi- ple times, to reduce test suite runtime. The only exception to this flow is users, which are always created and deleted between the tests of a test suite. User entities must always be new and unique to the test, to reduce failure and ease with debugging.

At the beginning and end of a program run, global setup and teardown initialise all entity registries by clearing them completely. The setup clear is a safety measure in the case that global teardown fails. This makes sure tests are pro- vided with fresh test data and that the unneeded seeded entities do not remain in the test environment as bloat.

In the test suites, fixtures are used to inject entity factories to the environment. Tests call the specific factory of the entity they require and, unless the test pa- rameters require creating a new entity, the factory begins initiating entity man- agement. It checks if the creation of the called entity is dependent on another entity and if yes, the factory calls that entity's registry to either find a pre-existing entity or create one. When dependencies have been solved, the factory calls the registry of its own entity and gives the same command to find or create.

The registry checks if an entity exists that matches the parameters set in the factory call. If one exists, the registry provides that seeded entity to the test. If not, the registry calls the client to create an API request to create one.

The client delegates payload population to the builder, which creates the pay- load based on the entity model and fills all empty values with default data. The payload is returned to the client, which utilises it to make an API request. Addi- tionally, the client waits and parses a request response for an entity ID or any errors.

The new entity, along with the ID, is passed back to the registry. It saves the seeded entity data into a test data file in the JSON format, for eventual removal via an API delete request. The seeded entity is then given to the test for use.

Originally, seeded entities required by the test and any higher-level entities they were dependent on would be created and deleted during each individual test run. Not only would this add to the runtime of a test, but the higher-level entities would also not do much more than exist to fulfil a creation condition. For exam- ple, one test suite might have six tests that all test the process of adding a prod- uct variant to the shopping cart. The test steps might be exactly the same ex- cept for one step of the process to account for different user behaviours.

While test data hygiene is critical, the automation team realised there was no need for this level of test data isolation inside a test suite. It would add to the run time per test, compounding over multiple tests. In cases like the example, there is no need for a new organisation, admin user and product each time.

Only creating a new variant that utilises already created high-level entities would suffice.

This led to the implementation of GlobalEntityRegistry that utilises entity specific registries to keep track of and manage all entities created within a run. For ex- ample, when a test calls for a variant and does not explicitly require the creation of a new product, the global registry checks using the corresponding entity reg- istry if a product already exists that could be used. If one does, it gets used. If one does not, the client is called to create one and the new entity is added to the global registry.

### Managing Test Flakiness

Test flakiness refers to tests failing occasionally without visible cause. E2E tests are inherently flaky, as they contain a multitude of dependencies, including net- work delays, third-party service outages and wait and locator errors. \[35.\]

Test flakiness can be managed and even reduced, if properly overseen. For ex- ample, timeout and wait errors can be reduced by implementing Playwright's smart wait functionality and locator failure by creating more robust and detailed locators. Occasionally, a test will randomly fail during an execution run and then run without issue when attempting to debug.

The aim is to not have any tests fail; the suites should have a success rate of over 95%. Sporadically failing tests and repeating error messages are docu- mented as an issue, so they can be resolved as soon as possible. While imple- menting test cases, the entire suite must be locally executed before attempting to merge to confirm system integration. Additionally, a test suite CI pipeline runs all tests on every push to branch. If a test fails, the run is considered failed. The run must pass before the development branch can be merged to the main branch.

# Future Development

The next phase will prioritize writing and implementing a new batch of P1 test cases. A new feature was pushed to production halfway through the project, creating fifteen new critical user stories to be defined. They could not be imple- mented in this phase and will be left for the next one. Additionally, new features will be developed and pushed to production over summer 2026, which will have to be prepared for.

Additionally, the process of granting the test automation team access to the de- velopment codebase will begin. This is an Objectives and Key Results (OKR) task for the second quarterly, increasing the probability of access being granted. This allows expanding the system to include new and pre-existing unit and inte- gration tests, instead of exclusively E2E.

Access to the codebase would also allow the implementation of continuous test automation by creating and integrating CI/CD pipelines. Although a general au- tomation pipeline already exists to execute all test suites when changes are made to the E2E test automation codebase, a CI/CD pipeline would support the whole test automation project by automatically executing full test automation once a day on a schedule and whenever changes are pushed to the test envi- ronment. This would give the product software developers quick feedback on any defects in the code, without the need of a human tester or manually execut- ing a program run command.

# Conclusion

The objective of this project was to design and implement a base test automa- tion system as well as to fulfil MVP requirements for critical test suites. The MVP requirements for the first phase were to ensure that at least 80% of critical test cases for both Kide.app and Kide.admin were designed and implemented, while providing the full development team access to the framework and estab- lishing clear documentation.

At the time of writing this conclusion, two of the three MVP requirements have been met. All team members have access to the test automation codebase and can execute automated tests locally. Additionally, the documentation provided was clear enough, and no issues arose during local setup. Kide.app test cover- age is exactly at the minimum requirement of 80% coverage. Kide.admin, while not yet at the goal coverage, has advanced significantly and reached 70% test coverage. With two weeks until the deadline, at the time of writing this, the ob- jective is possible to achieve.

During development, more detailed and comprehensive than originally planned test data management was implemented. The new data management logic keeps track of entities for the full run of a test suite and sends an API delete re- quest at the end of each program run for all created entities.

Although not planned for this phase, an automation pipeline was implemented for GitLab merge requests. The pipeline runs the whole system when a merge request is made and approves it if all test cases pass. It confirms that the new changes are properly integrated to the system and assist in managing test flaki- ness.

Overall, the results show that a strong foundation has been established for com- prehensive test automation at Treanglo. Manual testing will be reduced for E2E acceptance and release testing, saving human resources and energy. The ob- jectives of this project and thesis in general have been achieved.
